title: Hurricane Nolo: Slow, Strong, and Soaking Hawaii
summary:
A hurricane that barely moves can still be a disaster. Hurricane Nolo is proof. As of Friday afternoon, the storm was churning toward Hawaii at only 5 mph — slower than a person jogging — while its winds howled at 105 mph.

People on the Big Island are under a hurricane watch, meaning dangerous conditions could arrive within 24 to 36 hours. Nolo isn't expected to make landfall this weekend, but forecasters say that's almost beside the point. Its slow pace means it will linger, dumping enormous amounts of rain. Some areas could see more than 2 feet, with 10 to 25 inches expected more widely. The National Hurricane Center warned of "life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides."

Nolo is currently a Category 2 storm, but warm ocean waters could fuel it into a Category 4 with winds up to 140 mph over the next 72 hours. Maui is under a tropical storm watch and could get up to 10 inches of rain.

The storm's path has been unpredictable. Earlier this week, it was heading west across open ocean when it suddenly turned right, aiming north toward the Big Island. Just days before that, forecasters had declared the system was dissipating — then it regenerated into a hurricane.

This is the latest blow in a brutal year for Hawaii. In March, a Kona low caused the worst flooding in over two decades. A 6.0 magnitude earthquake shook the Big Island in May. Hurricane Lala raked the islands in August, and Hurricane Lowell pummeled Kauai earlier this month. Governor Josh Green said these four disasters alone have damaged or destroyed about 1,290 homes, with recovery costs estimated at roughly $1 billion before Nolo even arrives.

"We will pursue every available federal resource," Green said in a press release. Meanwhile, Nolo is part of a busy Pacific hurricane season fueled by a powerful El Niño. Three Category 5 storms — Genevieve, Lowell and Polo — have already formed. Hurricane season in Hawaii typically runs through November 30.
why_it_matters: How islands prepare for disasters — evacuation routes, stored supplies, insurance and federal aid — decides who recovers quickly and who is left waiting, and as ocean waters warm, slow soaking storms like Nolo are part of a pattern that will shape where and how people can safely live.

background_read: Hawaii is a chain of islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, far from any mainland, so supplies and emergency help have to travel a long way by ship or plane. In the early 1990s, Hurricane Iniki tore through Kauai and destroyed thousands of homes, changing how the islands plan for storms. Hurricane Lane in 2018 stalled near the Big Island and dropped record rainfall without ever making landfall — the same slow-motion threat Nolo poses now.

The National Hurricane Center (the US government office in Miami that tracks and names tropical storms) rates hurricanes from Category 1 to Category 5 based on wind speed, but most deaths in tropical systems come from water — flooding, mudslides and storm surge — rather than wind.

El Niño (a periodic warming of the eastern Pacific Ocean that shifts weather around the world) tends to boost hurricane activity in the Pacific while suppressing it in the Atlantic, which is why forecasters expect busy Pacific seasons in El Niño years.

perspectives.description: They argue that early watches and warnings are the whole point: giving residents a day or two to stock water, clear drains and prepare lets communities avoid the worst. Governor Josh Green's promise to pursue 'every available federal resource' reflects the same view — that fast warning and fast aid save lives.

They point to a year of back-to-back disasters and roughly $1 billion in recovery costs before Nolo even arrives, asking whether rebuilding is keeping pace and whether repeated damage is leaving some families behind. For them, the story is less about one storm than about a system that may be stretched thin.

They see Nolo as a textbook case of a shifting pattern: an El Niño-boosted Pacific season, unusually warm water that can upgrade a Category 2 to a Category 4, and storms that stall instead of sweeping through. They caution that single storms cannot prove a trend, but the combination of heat and slow motion is exactly what models project.

They focus on what changes next — stronger building codes, better drainage, moved roads and utilities, and clearer evacuation planning for islands with limited escape routes. The open question is whether Hawaii's rebuild will be designed for the storms it now expects rather than the ones it remembers.
